t: Points That Intersect With Cars — Marking / Difference Sweep
o: Cars occupy inclusive intervals [start, end] on the number line; count integer points covered by at least one car. In [[3,6],[1,5],[4,7]] the union spans 1..7, so 7 points. In [[1,3],[5,8]] the union is {1,2,3} ∪ {5,6,7,8}, also 7. Coordinates are bounded by 100 and there are at most 100 cars, so a boolean stamp array of size ~101 suffices.
k: Union of inclusive intervals: mark every integer in each interval and count marked cells.
A difference array gives the same answer in O(n + C) with C the coordinate range.

a.i: Allocate a boolean array over the coordinate domain, set true for every point inside any car's interval, then count trues. Dead simple and optimal at these sizes.
s: For each [s, e], mark seen[x] = true for x in [s, e].
Return the number of true entries.
a.t: O(n * C + C) — each car marks up to C = 100 points, then one counting pass.

a.i: Add +1 at each start and -1 just past each end, prefix-sum, and count positions with positive coverage. This scales to huge coordinate ranges (after coordinate compression) and many intervals, unlike direct stamping.
s: diff array of size 102; for [s,e]: diff[s]++, diff[e+1]--.
Count coordinates where the running coverage is positive.
a.t: O(n + C) — one pass to build diffs, one sweep over the coordinate range.

w: Stamping is the natural interview answer here; mention the difference array to show the scalable pattern for large coordinates. Pitfall: intervals are inclusive on both ends, so the decrement goes at e+1. Follow-up: report the merged disjoint intervals themselves (classic merge-intervals), or handle 2D rectangles.
